assignment.title: Solving Radical Equations — Honors
assignment.essentialQuestion: How does the structure of the equation influence the selection of an efficient method for solving equations involving rational exponents?
assignment.teacherNotes: Honors version of Bluebonnet Algebra II — Radicals, Lesson 4 (Solving Radical Equations), TEKS A2.7H (with A2.4F/A2.4G and A2.6B). Beyond the regular lesson: equations whose squared form has a fraction candidate, a graph that shows where extraneous candidates come from, rational exponents with even numerators (±) and even denominators (domain), two radicals that need two squarings, cube-root equations and why cubing is safe, parameters and no-solution cases decided by structure, and the horizon-distance model. Most single-radical equations are solved in the Sign & Solution Analyzer’s staged solver (isolate, raise, candidates, both sides of the ORIGINAL equation at every candidate, final answer), each stage graded on its own. Practice includes two audited SAT items (MathMaster CCMR bank). Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

questions.prompt: Solve $\sqrt{x + 4} + 2 = x$. Isolate the radical, square, solve the quadratic, and check both candidates in the original equation.

steps.title: Radical and rational-exponent equations
steps.instruction: 1. Isolate the radical (or the power). 2. Raise both sides to the index (for x^(m/n), use the power n/m, with ± when m is even). 3. Solve. 4. CHECK every candidate in the ORIGINAL equation.

steps.title: Extraneous candidates
steps.instruction: Raising both sides to an even power can add candidates that do not satisfy the original equation: a² = b² also holds when a = −b. An odd power never adds one.

steps.title: Decide by structure
steps.instruction: An isolated even root equal to a negative number has no real solution — no algebra needed.

responses.label: Where do y = √(x + 6) and y = x intersect?
The point (−2, −2) is where y = x meets…

responses.label: Why does squaring produce the candidate −2?
options: Squaring √(x + 6) = x and −√(x + 6) = x both give x + 6 = x², so the squared equation solves both
Squaring never adds solutions, so −2 is a real solution

(−√(x + 6))² is also x + 6.

solutionReview.headline: The squared equation describes both branches.
reasoning: y = √(x + 6) meets y = x only at (3, 3): √9 = 3.
Squaring cannot tell √(x + 6) = x from −√(x + 6) = x: both become x + 6 = x². That is where the extraneous candidate comes from.
x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2): its zeros 3 and −2 are the x-coordinates of the two intersections of y = x with the two branches.
solutionReview.commonError: Accepting −2 because it solves x + 6 = x²: that squared equation also describes y = −√(x + 6).

solutionReview.headline: Isolate, square, isolate, square — then check.
reasoning: Isolate: x + 1 = 2√(x + 1). Square: x² + 2x + 1 = 4(x + 1), so x² − 2x − 3 = 0 and x = 3 or x = −1.
Check: x = −1 gives √1 − √0 = 1, and x = 3 gives √9 − √4 = 1. Both are solutions.
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring each term separately: (1 + √(x + 1))² is not 1 + (x + 1).

questions.prompt: Odd index. Solve $\sqrt[3]{2x - 1} = \sqrt[3]{x + 4}$ and $\sqrt[3]{x^2 + 7} = 2$, then explain why cubing is safer than squaring.

responses.label: Why can cubing both sides never create an extraneous solution?
options: Cubing can be undone exactly: a³ = b³ only when a = b, unlike squaring
It can: cubing creates extraneous solutions as often as squaring
responses.answer: Cubing can be undone exactly: a³ = b³ only when a = b, unlike squaring

hints: Cube both sides of each equation.
For squaring, (−3)² = 3², so a² = b² does not force a = b.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If a³ = 8, then a equals…

solutionReview.headline: Cubing is reversible.
reasoning: Cube both sides: 2x − 1 = x + 4, so x = 5.
x² + 7 = 8, so x² = 1 and x = 1 or x = −1; both check, since ∛8 = 2.
a³ = b³ forces a = b, so cubing never adds a solution; a² = b² allows a = −b, which is why squaring can.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting the negative solution: x² = 1 gives x = 1 or x = −1, and both check because cubing can be undone.

questions.prompt: Decide by structure, before any algebra. Sort each equation.

categories.label: No real solution: an even root equals a negative number
Check needed: an even power can create extraneous candidates

hints: Isolate the root in your head: is an even root being set equal to a negative number?
Raising both sides to an even power can add candidates; an odd power cannot.

solutionReview.headline: Isolate the root, then read its index and the sign of the other side.
reasoning: No real solution: √(x + 2) = −5, (x + 1)^(1/4) = −2 and √(3x) = −4 each set an even root equal to a negative number, and an even root is never negative.
Check needed: √(x + 5) = x − 1, √(2x + 1) = x − 7 and ∜(x + 12) = x are raised to an even power, which can add a candidate where the right side is negative (x = −1 in the first, x = 4 in the second).
Odd index: ∛(x − 1) = −2, ∛(x + 6) = x and (x − 3)^(1/5) = −1. Cubing, or raising to the fifth power, can be undone, so no candidate is extraneous.
solutionReview.answerSummary: No real solution: √(x + 2) = −5, (x + 1)^(1/4) + 3 = 1, √(3x) + 4 = 0. Check needed: √(x + 5) = x − 1, √(2x + 1) = x − 7, ∜(x + 12) = x. Odd index: the other three.
solutionReview.commonError: ∛(x − 1) = −2 has a solution: an odd root can be negative, so only an even root set equal to a negative number has none.

reasoning: x = {{p}} is a solution, so √({{p}} + k) = {{p}} − {{b}} = {{r}}.
Square both sides: {{p}} + k = {{r}}², so k = {{r}}² − {{p}} = {{k}}.
The right side {{p}} − {{b}} = {{r}} is positive, so it can equal a square root: the solution checks.
